3810: A curator is a person who carefully selects, organizes, and takes care of a collection — and then presents it meaningfully to others.

Think of a museum. It doesn't just dump thousands of objects into a room. Someone had to decide: Which paintings belong here? In what order should visitors see them? What story does this collection tell? That person is the curator.

A curator is an expert caretaker and selector. The job has three inseparable parts:

  1. Selecting — choosing what belongs in the collection and what doesn't (this requires deep knowledge and judgment)
  2. Organizing and preserving — arranging, protecting, and maintaining what's in the collection
  3. Presenting — making the collection meaningful and accessible to an audience

Notice that all three parts involve doing something for others, not just for yourself. This is important — a curator's entire purpose is to serve an audience. That's what separates a curator from someone who just collects things privately.
The classic setting: museums and institutions

The word is most traditionally tied to museums, art galleries, libraries, archives, and similar institutions.

A museum curator of ancient Roman history, for example, might spend years researching which Roman coins, sculptures, and everyday objects best represent life in that era. They write the descriptions on the wall plaques. They decide that a cracked, weathered pottery bowl is actually more historically revealing than a perfect, shiny one, so they choose that one. They arrange the room so visitors naturally move through history in a logical order. They ensure the artifacts are stored safely so they survive for the next hundred years.

This curator is not just a caretaker in the sense of a security guard. They are an intellectual authority. Their expertise shapes what people see, how they see it, and what they're supposed to understand from it.

Over time, the word has expanded far beyond museums, and today it's used in many contexts — all of which preserve that same core idea of expert selection and meaningful organization for an audience.

A music curator selects songs for a playlist with a specific mood or purpose. The playlists you see on Spotify labelled "Focus," "Rainy Day," or "Road Trip" are assembled by curators who understand music deeply and make deliberate choices about what fits and what doesn't.

A content curator (common in digital media and journalism) sifts through the overwhelming flood of online articles, videos, and social media posts to find what's genuinely valuable, and packages it for their audience — a daily newsletter of the best reads, for example.

An exhibition curator (in art) might not even work for a museum permanently. They might be brought in specifically to design and build a temporary exhibition. They choose the theme, select specific works by various artists, and create the narrative experience of walking through the show.

A data curator (in technology and science) manages datasets — deciding which data is reliable, how it should be organized, and how it should be documented so others can use it accurately.

The setting changes, but the pattern never does: expertise + selection + organization + serving an audience.
What makes a curator different from a collector?

This is a subtle but important distinction.

A collector gathers things for personal enjoyment, passion, or investment. The collection is mainly for them. There's no obligation to explain it, share it, or make it meaningful to anyone else.

A curator gathers, organizes, and presents things for others. The collection exists to serve an audience — to educate, inspire, preserve cultural memory, or help people make sense of something. The curator acts as a bridge between the collection and the people who experience it.

Also, a collector might simply accumulate — buying everything available. A curator must exclude. In fact, the act of saying "this belongs here, but this does not" is central to curation. It requires judgment. A poor curator includes everything indiscriminately. A great curator makes each item in the collection feel essential.

One more important layer: calling someone a curator implies that they have earned the right to make these selections. They're not just anyone who picked a few things — they're recognized as knowledgeable enough that their judgment is trusted. When a major art gallery's curator chooses a painting, that choice carries weight. It signals to the art world: this matters.

This is why the word has a certain prestige to it. And it's also why the word is sometimes used loosely or even criticized in casual contexts — calling yourself a "curator" of your Instagram feed, for instance, can feel like borrowing that prestige without truly earning it.

A curator is a trusted expert who carefully selects what belongs in a collection, organizes and preserves it, and presents it in a way that is meaningful and valuable to an audience — whether that collection consists of ancient artifacts in a museum, songs in a playlist, articles in a newsletter, or data in a scientific database.
3811: The word "curb" as a noun has two main meanings. The first is a physical object you encounter in daily life. The second is a concept about control or limitation. There is also a third, more specialized meaning from horse riding.
Meaning 1: The Edge Between a Sidewalk and a Road

This is by far the most common meaning.

A curb is the raised border — usually made of concrete, stone, or granite — that runs along the outer edge of a sidewalk where the sidewalk meets the road. Imagine you are walking on a sidewalk and you want to cross the street. You reach the edge of the sidewalk and step down onto the road. That small step-down structure you move across is the curb. It is a kind of low wall or ledge — usually about 15 to 20 centimetres (roughly 6 to 8 inches) high — that separates the pedestrian walking area from the vehicle road.

It is not just decorative. A curb serves real purposes:

  • It stops vehicles from accidentally drifting onto the sidewalk.
  • It channels rainwater along the road and into drainage systems instead of letting it flood the sidewalk.
  • It gives pedestrians a clear, physical signal of where it is safe to walk and where traffic moves.

In British English, this same physical structure is spelled "kerb" — a completely different spelling but exactly the same object and meaning. So if you ever read British books, newspapers, or websites, you will see "kerb" rather than "curb." Both refer to the same thing.

Example sentences:

  • "She sat on the curb, waiting for the bus."
  • "The driver pulled the car to the curb and stopped."
  • "Be careful when you step off the curb — a car is coming."
  • "The dog sat obediently at the curb while his owner looked both ways."

Common phrases and compound words built from this meaning:

Curb appeal
The visual attractiveness of a building or property as seen from the street — in other words, from the curb. This phrase is most commonly used in real estate. A house with strong curb appeal looks well-maintained, welcoming, and attractive just from the outside, before anyone even walks through the door.

"They planted flowers and repainted the shutters to improve the house's curb appeal."

Curbside (also written curb-side)
The area right beside the curb — the part of the road that borders the sidewalk. The word is used especially in the phrase curbside pickup, which became extremely common during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. It means you place an order (at a restaurant, a pharmacy, a grocery store), drive to the location, park near the curb, and a staff member brings your items directly to your car. You never have to go inside.

"The pharmacy offers curbside pickup for prescriptions."
"The taxi pulled up curbside to collect the passengers."

Curb cut
A curb cut is a small ramp or slope built into the curb, so that someone in a wheelchair, pushing a stroller, riding a bicycle, or pulling a cart can smoothly move from the sidewalk to the road without having to step over the curb. In British English, this is often called a dropped curb or dropped kerb.

"The curb cut made it easy for the wheelchair user to cross at the intersection."

Curb lane
The lane of traffic that runs along the outermost edge of the road — the lane closest to the curb. Buses typically pick up and drop off passengers from the curb lane.

"The cyclist stayed in the curb lane to avoid faster traffic."
Meaning 2: A Restraint, Check, or Limitation

This is the second major meaning of "curb" as a noun, and it is more abstract. Here, a "curb" means something — a rule, a law, a force, an action — that holds something else back, keeps it under control, or prevents it from going too far.

Think of it this way: if a problem, a behavior, or a force is growing, increasing, or getting out of hand, a "curb" is what is placed on it to slow it down, limit it, or bring it back under control.

The standard phrase to know is: "a curb on [something]" — meaning a restriction or check placed on that thing.

Example sentences:

  • "The new regulations served as a curb on pollution." — The regulations restricted or controlled how much pollution was produced.
  • "The central bank raised interest rates as a curb on inflation." — Higher interest rates were used as a tool to slow down inflation.
  • "There must be a stronger curb on the power of large corporations." — There must be stronger controls or limits placed on corporate power.
  • "The treaty placed curbs on the production of nuclear weapons." — The treaty imposed restrictions on nuclear weapons production.
  • "His sense of responsibility acted as a curb on his wilder impulses." — His responsibility held back his more reckless tendencies.

You will see this meaning frequently in journalism, politics, economics, and formal writing. It can appear in the singular ("a curb on") or the plural ("curbs on").

Other words that mean something similar: a check, a restraint, a restriction, a limit, a brake (used figuratively), a control.
Meaning 3: A Piece of Horse-Riding Equipment

This is a technical, specialized meaning. You are unlikely to use it in everyday conversation, but you may encounter it in books, historical texts, or content about horse riding.

In equestrian (horse-riding) contexts, a curb — also called a curb bit or curb chain — is a piece of metal equipment used to control a horse. It is a chain or bar that fits under the horse's lower jaw as part of the bridle (the set of straps placed over a horse's head). When the rider pulls the reins, the curb presses against the horse's jaw and the groove under its chin, applying pressure to help steer and slow the horse. It is a tool of direct physical control.

"The trainer attached the curb chain carefully to the horse's bridle."
"A curb bit gives the rider more precise control over a powerful horse."

This is also the historical origin of the "restraint" meaning above — a curb was originally a physical device used to control something powerful (a horse), and over time the word came to describe any kind of restraint or check.
Summary of All Meanings at a Glance

Physical boundaryThe raised concrete or stone edge at the side of a road, separating the sidewalk from the street. (British spelling: kerb)
A restraint or limitSomething that holds back, controls, or restricts a force, behavior, or trend. Used in the phrase "a curb on [something]."
Horse equipmentA chain or bar fitted under a horse's jaw to help a rider control the animal. (Specialized use)
One Final Thought: How the Meanings Relate

Notice that all three meanings share a common thread: the idea of a boundary or control. The physical curb creates a boundary between sidewalk and road. The "restraint" curb creates a boundary between acceptable and excessive. The horse's curb chain creates a boundary between the horse going where it wants and going where the rider wants. Once you see that underlying idea of boundary-setting and control, the word "curb" in any context will immediately make sense to you.
3812:
When a smooth liquid — most commonly milk or cream — breaks apart into thick, lumpy solid bits floating in a thin, watery liquid, we say it has curdled. The solid bits are called curds, and the remaining watery liquid is called whey. So "curdle" literally means: to transform a smooth liquid into separated, lumpy solids and thin liquid.

Think of it this way: imagine a glass of fresh, smooth milk. Now imagine leaving it out for too long. It turns sour, and you notice gross lumps floating in it — it no longer looks smooth and uniform. That milk has curdled.
The Two Directions of the Word

"Curdle" can be used in two ways:

1. Without an object (intransitive) — something curdles on its own:
The subject itself undergoes the change.

"The milk curdled in the heat."
"The cream curdled when she added the lemon juice."
"The sauce curdled because the heat was too high."

2. With an object (transitive) — something causes another thing to curdle:
One thing acts on another to make it curdle.

"The acid curdled the milk."
"Too much heat will curdle your custard."

You don't need to know chemistry deeply, but it helps to understand the basic triggers:

  • Acid — Adding something acidic (like lemon juice or vinegar) to milk or cream can break it apart and cause it to curdle. In fact, cheesemakers do this on purpose to make cheese. The curds are collected and pressed; that's your cheese. The leftover watery liquid (whey) is separated off.
  • Heat — High or uneven heat can cause dairy-based sauces and custards to curdle, ruining their smooth texture.
  • Age/Spoilage — When milk goes bad naturally over time, bacteria produce acid, which causes the milk to curdle on its own.

So curdling isn't always an accident — it's sometimes intentional. Yogurt, cheese, and paneer are all made by deliberately curdling milk.
Figurative Meaning: When Good Things Go Bad

Beyond the kitchen, "curdle" is also used figuratively to describe something that was once smooth, pleasant, or good — but has slowly turned sour, dark, or bad. Just like milk goes from fresh to spoiled, a feeling, relationship, or situation can "curdle" over time.

"His admiration for her slowly curdled into jealousy."

(What was once a positive feeling — admiration — turned into something unpleasant.)

"The friendship had curdled after years of small betrayals."

(A warm relationship deteriorated and turned bitter.)

"What started as excitement curdled into dread."

(A good feeling transformed into a bad one.)

The figurative use almost always carries this sense of a gradual, unwanted transformation from something good or neutral into something unpleasant or corrupted. The image of fresh milk slowly souring is the perfect mental picture for this meaning too.

One of the most famous uses of this word is the phrase "blood-curdling" (also written as "blood curdling").

Historically, people believed that extreme terror could literally thicken or clot a person's blood — just like milk curdles. So when something is so horrifying, shocking, or frightening that it feels like it stops your blood cold, we call it blood-curdling.

"We heard a blood-curdling scream from the next room."
"The movie was full of blood-curdling scenes."

You can also say:

"The sound made my blood curdle."

It means: "It terrified me deeply."

This is a fixed idiomatic expression — you wouldn't use it to describe mild fear, only extreme, visceral horror or shock.
Quick Summary of All the Ways "Curdle" Is Used

SenseWhat it meansExample

Literally, curdle means for a liquid (usually dairy) to separate into lumpy solids and thin watery liquid — either because of acid, heat, or spoilage.

In cooking, it usually refers to something going wrong (a sauce breaking, a custard splitting), though it can be intentional when making cheese or yogurt.

Figuratively, it means for something to slowly go from good or neutral to sour, bitter, or dark — like feelings, relationships, or situations.

Idiomatically, "blood-curdling" or "make one's blood curdle" means to cause extreme horror or terror.
Helpful Sentences to Lock It In

• "The recipe says don't let the sauce curdle — keep the heat low."
  • "She opened the carton and saw that the milk had curdled."
  • "His trust in his partner slowly curdled into suspicion."
  • "It was a blood-curdling howl that woke the whole neighborhood."
  • "Adding lemon juice too quickly will curdle the cream."

The through-line in every single use — literal or figurative — is the same idea: something that was once smooth and whole has broken down and turned unpleasant. Keep that image in mind, and you'll understand "curdle" in any context you ever encounter it.
3813:
To understand curdled, you first need to picture what happens to milk when it goes bad — or when something (like lemon juice or heat) is added to it. The milk, which was smooth and evenly mixed, suddenly separates. It breaks apart into two things: soft, lumpy white solids (called curds) and a thin, watery liquid. That ruined, lumpy, separated state is what curdled describes.

So curdled means: something that was once smooth and unified has broken apart into an unpleasant, separated, lumpy mess — and in doing so, has also become unfit, wrong, or spoiled.

As an adjective, curdled describes any liquid — most often milk, cream, or a sauce — that has broken down into lumps floating in watery liquid.

  • Curdled milk is milk that has soured and clumped. It smells sour, looks uneven and lumpy, and is no longer smooth.
  • Curdled cream or a curdled sauce describes the same kind of breakdown — what was once silky and homogeneous has split into an ugly, grainy texture.

The key qualities of something curdled:

  • It was once smooth, even, and properly mixed
  • Something went wrong (heat, acid, bacteria, time)
  • It has now separated into a broken, clumped state
  • It is generally unpleasant, unappetising, or ruined

This is where curdled becomes especially interesting. Because of what it means physically — something good turning bad and separating — it is widely used as a metaphor for anything that has soured, turned wrong, or decayed from what it once was.

Think of it this way: just as good milk can curdle into something unpleasant, good things in life can "curdle" too.

Examples:

  • A curdled friendship — a friendship that was once warm and close but has turned sour, become strained or bitter, and is now broken or unpleasant.
  • A curdled smile — a smile that has gone wrong; it started as something pleasant but twisted into something forced, bitter, or ugly — like someone trying to smile but it comes out looking like a sneer or a grimace.
  • A curdled dream — a hope or ambition that once felt bright and promising but has turned into something bitter, failed, or corrupted.
  • The atmosphere in the room curdled — the mood, which may have been fine, has suddenly turned uncomfortable, tense, or unpleasant.
  • Admiration that has curdled into resentment — what was once genuine admiration has soured and transformed into something negative.

In all these cases, curdled carries the same emotional weight: something that was good, clean, or unified has broken down into something bad, bitter, or wrong.

You may encounter curdled in descriptions of extreme fear or horror — most famously in the related word blood-curdling (meaning something so terrifying it feels like it makes your blood curdle, i.e., freeze and thicken with fear). While blood-curdling is the more common compound, you can also encounter curdled on its own in descriptions of horror, disgust, or dread:

  • A curdled feeling in his stomach — a feeling of dread or nausea, as though something inside has gone sour.
  • Her blood curdled at the sight — she felt a wave of cold, paralyzing terror.

This usage leans on the physical idea that extreme fear causes the blood to "clump" or "seize up," just as milk curdles.
The Underlying Tone: Corruption and Wrongness

What all uses of curdled share is a sense of something gone irreversibly wrong. It is not just "bad" — it is specifically the kind of bad that comes from something that was good. There is always an implied "before" in the word: a time when things were smooth, pure, or pleasant. Curdled marks the point of no return, the spoiling.

This makes it a word with a slightly bleak, melancholic tone. Something curdled is not just broken — it is a reminder of what it once was.

ContextWhat "curdled" describes
  • Milk/cream/sauce: Separated into lumps and watery liquid; spoiled and broken down
  • Relationships/feelings: Once good, now gone sour, bitter, or broken
  • Dreams/ideals: Once promising, now failed or corrupted
  • Moods/atmospheres: Turned tense, unpleasant, or hostile
  • Fear/horror: A frozen, sick, physically unpleasant sensation
A Few Sentences to Cement It

• She poured the curdled milk down the sink — it had gone off overnight.
  • What began as a playful rivalry had curdled into genuine hatred over the years.
  • He gave a curdled smile — polite on the surface, but full of bitterness underneath.
  • The childhood dream of becoming a musician had curdled somewhere in his twenties, replaced by cynicism.
  • The happy mood of the party curdled the moment the argument broke out.

In short: curdled always points to something that has broken from smooth wholeness into a sour, separated, unpleasant state — whether that's milk in a glass or warmth in a heart.
3814:
A cure is something that completely removes or eliminates a disease, illness, or problem — not just eases it, but actually gets rid of it.

This "completely" is the heart of the word. A cure doesn't just make you feel better temporarily; it fixes the root cause and ends the problem.
The Most Common Meaning: In Health and Medicine

In medicine, a cure is a medicine, treatment, or procedure that fully and permanently eliminates a disease from a person's body.

"Scientists have been searching for a cure for cancer for decades."
"Penicillin was the cure for many deadly bacterial infections."
"There is currently no cure for Alzheimer's disease."

Notice how in these sentences, "cure" refers to whatever completely defeats the disease — it could be a drug, a therapy, a surgical procedure, or anything else.

The Single Most Important Distinction: Cure vs. Treatment

This is something many people confuse, and understanding it will make the word much clearer to you.

  • A treatment manages a disease — it controls its symptoms, slows it down, or reduces its harm. But the disease is still there.
  • A cure ends the disease entirely. After a cure, the disease is gone.

Think of HIV/AIDS as an example. Today, there are highly effective medicines for HIV. A person with HIV can take these medicines and live a completely normal, long, healthy life. These medicines are called treatments — not a cure. Why? Because the virus is still present in the body; the medicines just keep it suppressed. If the person stops taking the medicine, the virus comes back. A cure would mean the virus is fully eliminated from the body forever, so the person no longer needs any medicine. That cure does not yet exist.

Another example: the common cold. When you have a cold, you might take medicines that reduce your fever, ease your stuffy nose, or soothe your sore throat. These are treatments. They don't cure the cold — your immune system itself eventually cures it, by fighting off the virus completely.

So remember: treatment = managing the problem; cure = ending it.

"Cure" Can Refer to the Actual Substance or Method

The word "cure" can point to the specific thing (medicine, therapy, procedure) that achieves the healing:

"Vitamin C is the cure for scurvy."

Here, vitamin C is the cure — it's the actual thing that fixes the problem (scurvy is a disease caused by lack of vitamin C, and simply consuming vitamin C makes it completely go away).
The Broader Meaning: A Solution to Any Problem

"Cure" is also used outside of medicine to mean a solution that fixes or resolves any kind of problem, not just a health issue.

"There is no easy cure for loneliness."
"Rest is the best cure for exhaustion."
"Education is often called the cure for ignorance."

In these cases, the logic is the same — a cure is something that removes or resolves the problem at its source, not just masks it. You'll use this meaning whenever you're speaking about non-medical problems.

"Cure" as a noun also appears in the context of preserving food, especially meat, fish, or cheese. Here, the cure refers to the substance or process used to preserve the food — usually involving salt, sugar, smoke, or a combination of these. The preserving agent is sometimes called "the cure."

"The ham was given a dry cure before being smoked."
"A salt-and-sugar cure is applied to the salmon for 48 hours."

The idea behind using "cure" here is that the preservation process "treats" the food so it doesn't spoil — it's a metaphorical borrowing from the medical world.
In Religious or Ecclesiastical Context (Specialized, Rare)

This meaning is specialized and old-fashioned, but you may encounter it in literature or formal writing. In the context of the Christian church, "cure" (especially in the phrase "cure of souls") means the spiritual care and responsibility a priest or pastor has for the people of their parish.

"The young priest took up his cure in a small rural village."

This usage is rare in everyday English today, but you'll find it in older texts or formal church writing.

"No cure" doesn't mean no hope. When people say a disease has "no cure," it doesn't mean it's untreatable. Many diseases with no cure — HIV, diabetes, many mental illnesses — are managed very effectively with treatments. People with these conditions live full lives. "No cure" simply means the disease cannot currently be permanently eliminated.

A cure is often an outcome, not just a thing. Sometimes the word refers to the state of being completely healed, rather than the specific medicine that caused it.

"After years of treatment, she finally achieved a complete cure."

Here, "cure" is the result — the state of full recovery.

• "A cure for what ails you" — informal for something that fixes your problem, whatever it is. Often used humorously or warmly.
  • "The cure is worse than the disease" — a saying used when a solution causes more harm than the original problem it was meant to fix.
  • "Cure-all" — a single remedy claimed to fix everything. Usually said with skepticism, since nothing truly cures all things. "He sold this herb as a cure-all, but it was pure nonsense."
  • "Beyond cure" — too damaged or far gone to be fixed. Can be used literally (a disease) or figuratively (a hopeless situation or person).

ContextWhat "cure" means

"Cure" in noun form always carries the same core idea: a complete, definitive fix. In medicine, it means a remedy that fully eliminates a disease. Broadly, it means any solution that truly resolves a problem — not just covers it up. In food, it refers to the preserving treatment applied to food. In old church language, it means pastoral care of a parish. In all cases, the word points to something that doesn't just manage or soothe — it actually resolves and ends whatever problem it's directed at.
3815: A curfew is a rule or official order that restricts people from being in public spaces — streets, parks, or any outdoor area — during certain hours, usually at night. It is essentially a "stay indoors" command. The word can refer both to the rule itself and to the specific time at which that rule kicks in.

1. In government, law, and public order (the formal sense)

This is the most serious use of the word. A government, military authority, or law enforcement agency issues a curfew telling everyone that between certain hours — say, 9 PM to 6 AM — no one may be on the streets or in public without a valid reason. Anyone found outside during those hours can be arrested, fined, or penalized.

Curfews in this sense are almost always temporary and are declared during situations of crisis or danger, such as:

  • Wars or military occupations
  • Civil unrest, riots, or large-scale protests
  • Natural disasters (floods, earthquakes)
  • Pandemics or public health emergencies

The aim is typically to restore order, prevent violence or looting, protect civilians, or allow authorities to operate more effectively when the streets are empty.

2. In families and parenting (the informal sense)

Here, a curfew is a time set by a parent telling their child when they must be home by. If a parent says, "Your curfew is 10 PM," the child is expected to return home at or before 10 PM. Coming home after that time means the child has broken their curfew, which typically leads to some form of punishment.

Same underlying principle as the formal sense — a time-based restriction — just at a household level.

3. Institutional curfews

Schools, hostels, and boarding institutions also impose curfews on students, requiring them to be inside the building by a specific time. These sit somewhere between the governmental and parental sense in terms of formality.
"Curfew" = Both the Rule and the Time

This is a subtle but important point. The word doesn't just mean the rule — it also refers to the specific hour at which the restriction begins (or the entire restricted period).

  • "The curfew is at 8 PM" → the restriction starts at 8 PM.
  • "I have to leave before curfew" → I need to leave before the restricted hours begin.
  • "Curfew ends at 6 AM" → freedom to go outside is restored at 6 AM.
  • "My curfew is 11" → I must be home by 11 PM.

So depending on context, "curfew" fluidly refers to the order itself or to the time associated with it.

A curfew is always temporary. It is not a permanent law. It operates on a schedule — either recurring daily ("every night from 9 PM to 5 AM") or for a fixed period ("for the next 10 days"). Once the crisis is over, or the period ends, the curfew is lifted.

A curfew restricts movement, not all activity. It controls whether you can be outside in public spaces. What you do inside your home is unaffected.

A curfew applies to a group, not just one person. It targets everyone within a defined area or category — a city, a country, all students in a hostel, all minors in a town. This distinguishes it from house arrest, which is a restriction placed on one specific individual.

Some curfews apply only to certain groups. For example, some cities have juvenile curfews — laws that restrict only minors (people under 18) from being out on streets past a certain hour, while adults are free to move around.

These are the most common word combinations you'll encounter:

  • Impose / declare a curfew — to officially put a curfew into effect
    "The military imposed a curfew after the protests turned violent."
  • Lift / end / ease a curfew — to officially remove or relax a curfew
    "The government lifted the curfew once order was restored."
  • Enforce a curfew — to actively ensure people are following it
    "Police were out in force, enforcing the curfew."
  • Break / violate a curfew — to disobey the curfew by being outside during restricted hours
    "Dozens of people were arrested for breaking the curfew."
  • Miss / beat curfew — in the family context, to arrive home after (or just before) the set time
    "She missed curfew by 20 minutes and lost her phone privileges for a week."
  • Under curfew — in a state where a curfew is currently active
    "The entire city was under curfew for five days."
  • Curfew hours — the specific span of time during which the curfew is in effect
    "All shops must be closed during curfew hours."
  • Curfew order — the formal, official document or command that establishes a curfew

1. The government declared a curfew from 10 PM to 5 AM following the outbreak of unrest.
  2. Soldiers patrolled empty streets to make sure everyone was observing the curfew.
  3. The curfew was lifted after three days, and life slowly returned to normal.
  4. Anyone found outdoors after curfew would be detained and questioned.
  5. My parents gave me a curfew of 9:30 PM on weeknights.
  6. He broke his curfew and came home at midnight — his parents were furious.
  7. The town has had a juvenile curfew for years — kids under 16 cannot be out past 10 PM.
  8. "What time is your curfew?" "I have to be back by 11."

AspectDetail

In short: A curfew is a time-based restriction on movement — an order telling people they must be off the streets and indoors between certain hours. It can be issued by a government during a crisis, by a school or hostel for students, or by a parent for their child. The word refers both to the rule itself and to the time it takes effect. It is always temporary, always applies to a group, and restricts movement in public — not what happens indoors. Breaking a curfew means being outside when you're not allowed to be, and it carries consequences ranging from grounding (at home) to arrest (under governmental curfews).
3816:
A curio is a small, unusual object that people find interesting or fascinating — often because it is rare, old, exotic, or just plain strange. It's the kind of thing you might pick up, turn over in your hands, and wonder about.

Think of it this way: imagine you walk into an old shop and notice a tiny ivory elephant carved in India a century ago, a glass bottle of Victorian-era smelling salts, and a compass that once belonged to a sailor. Those would all be curios. Each is interesting not because it is useful, but because it has a quality that makes you stop and look twice.

A curio typically has one or more of these qualities:

  • It is rare — you don't see it every day
  • It is old or antique
  • It comes from a faraway place or culture
  • It has an unusual shape, history, or origin
  • It makes you ask, "What is this? Where did it come from?"

A curio is almost always a physical, tangible object — something you can hold or display. It is typically small enough to fit on a shelf or in a cabinet, not a large piece of furniture or machinery.

One of the most important things about the word "curio" is the feeling it implies. When something is called a curio, there's a sense of wonder, curiosity, and quiet delight attached to it. The object feels like it has a story — a past, a mystery, a life before it ended up in front of you.

This is what separates a curio from something that is merely old or merely foreign. A cracked old spoon is not a curio. But a tiny silver snuff box engraved with a mysterious monogram and the initials of someone long dead? That could very well be one.

• "The antique shop was cluttered with curios from every corner of the world."
  • "She displayed her curios on a velvet-lined shelf — a fossilized shark tooth, a miniature Moroccan lantern, and a Victorian mourning brooch."
  • "He couldn't pass a flea market without hunting for curios to add to his collection."
  • "The museum's back room held a collection of curios that didn't fit neatly into any official exhibit."

You will very often hear the phrase curio cabinet. This is a glass-fronted display cabinet made specifically for showing off a collection of curios. If you've ever seen a tall cabinet with glass panels in an older home — filled with small figurines, old coins, shells, delicate china, and other interesting objects — that is a curio cabinet. It is common enough that furniture stores sell them by this exact name.
What a curio is NOT — and how it differs from similar words

Curio vs. knick-knack: A knick-knack is a small decorative object, but it doesn't carry the same sense of rarity or fascination. Knick-knacks are often cheap and mass-produced. Curios feel more special — they have a certain distinction.

Curio vs. antique: An antique is simply something old (usually 100+ years). But a curio doesn't have to be old — what makes it a curio is its interesting, unusual nature, not just its age. All antiques are not curios, and technically, a curio need not be an antique.

Curio vs. artifact: An artifact is usually associated with historical or archaeological significance and is a more formal, academic word (think museum exhibits or excavations). A curio is more personal — it's something an individual collects, displays, and treasures.

Curio vs. collectible: A collectible is anything people collect in series (stamps, trading cards, coins). A curio is specifically an object that stands out for being unusual or interesting — it doesn't need to be part of a set or series.
The tone and feel of the word

"Curio" has a slightly old-fashioned, literary quality to it. It carries a sense of refinement and wonder. You are more likely to encounter it in an antique shop, a museum, or a novel than in everyday casual speech. When someone uses the word "curio," they are suggesting that the object in question has a certain dignity and mystique — it is not junk, it is not ordinary, it is something worth pausing over and appreciating.
A curio is a small, unusual, often rare or exotic object that people collect and treasure because it is genuinely interesting, strange, or beautiful in a way that ordinary objects are not.
3817:
Curiosity is a strong, active desire to know, learn, or understand something. It is the inner feeling — almost like a pull or an itch — that makes you want to find out more about something unknown, puzzling, or interesting. When you feel curiosity, you are not satisfied just sitting with a question; you want an answer. You want to explore, investigate, ask, or dig deeper.

Think of it this way: imagine you walk past a closed door and you hear strange sounds from inside. That immediate, almost involuntary feeling of "What's in there? I need to find out" — that is curiosity.
What Curiosity Feels Like From the Inside

Curiosity is not a passive feeling. It has a kind of energy to it. When you are curious about something, you feel a gap — a gap between what you currently know and what you want to know. That gap is uncomfortable in a pleasant, motivating way. It pushes you toward finding answers.

This is why curious people ask questions, explore new places, read books, conduct experiments, and look things up. Curiosity is the engine behind learning and discovery.
The Two Main Senses of the Word

1. Curiosity as a feeling or state of mind (uncountable noun)

This is the most common use. Here, "curiosity" refers to the emotion or quality of wanting to know or understand. It has no plural in this sense because it describes a state, not a thing you can count.

  • "She approached every new subject with great curiosity."
  • "The child stared at the magician with wide-eyed curiosity."
  • "Out of curiosity, I decided to try the strange dish." (This phrase — "out of curiosity" — means doing something simply to satisfy your desire to know, not for any practical reason.)

2. A curiosity — an unusual or rare object, person, or thing (countable noun)

When you say someone or something is "a curiosity," or talk about "curiosities" (plural), you mean something strange, rare, or unusual that attracts attention and makes people want to look at it or know more about it. Antique shops are sometimes called "curiosity shops" because they sell unusual, old, or peculiar objects that fascinate people.

  • "The two-headed coin was a curiosity that everyone wanted to examine."
  • "He collected curiosities from his travels — odd little objects from different cultures."
  • "To the other children, the new boy was something of a curiosity because he had never seen a television."

In this second sense, the word simply means: something that is interesting precisely because it is unusual or difficult to explain.

Curiosity is not always the same intensity. It can range from a very light, passing interest to a deep, almost consuming need to know. The English language captures these differences with phrases that modify "curiosity":

  • Idle curiosity — mild, casual curiosity with no real urgency. You are mildly interested but would not go out of your way to find an answer. "I wondered idly, out of nothing more than idle curiosity, who had built that wall."
  • Burning curiosity / intense curiosity — a very strong, urgent need to know. The question feels impossible to ignore. "She had a burning curiosity about her grandfather's past and spent years researching it."
  • Intellectual curiosity — a desire to understand ideas, theories, concepts, and how things work at a deeper level. People who are intellectually curious love thinking, asking "why," and exploring complex topics. This is often considered a very positive trait in students, scientists, and thinkers.
  • Natural curiosity — the curiosity that humans (especially children) are born with; an inborn tendency to explore and question the world. "Children have a natural curiosity that adults sometimes forget to keep alive."
  • Morbid curiosity — a fascination with things that are dark, disturbing, grim, or unpleasant — like wanting to look at an accident scene even though you know it might upset you. The word "morbid" here signals that this type of curiosity feels slightly unhealthy or uncomfortable to have, even if it is very human and common.

Curiosity can be pointed toward virtually anything:

  • People — wanting to know about someone's life, background, thoughts, or feelings
  • Places — wanting to explore somewhere you have never been
  • Ideas and knowledge — wanting to understand how something works, why something happens, or what something means
  • Mysteries and unknowns — anything that has not been explained
  • Other people's private lives — this edge of curiosity, when pushed too far, becomes nosiness or prying, which carry negative social judgments. Curiosity in itself is neutral to positive; but when you apply it intrusively to others' private affairs without their welcome, it shades into something most people find rude.

It helps to know what curiosity is different from:

  • Interest is close to curiosity, but softer. You can be interested in something and feel no urgency about it. Curiosity has more of an active, forward-leaning quality — it makes you do something to find out.
  • Fascination is when something holds your attention completely, almost involuntarily. Fascination is what you feel when you cannot look away. Curiosity is more about wanting to know; fascination is about being held or captured by something.
  • Wonder is a sense of awe or amazement — you feel small or astonished in front of something vast or beautiful. Curiosity is about wanting information; wonder is more about the emotional experience of encountering something extraordinary. The two feelings often appear together.
  • Obsession is much more extreme and tends to be unhealthy. Curiosity motivates exploration and learning; obsession takes over and distorts thinking and behavior.
How Curiosity Is Commonly Expressed in Language

Certain phrases with "curiosity" appear very frequently in English. Knowing them will help you use and recognize the word naturally:

  • "Out of curiosity" — doing something purely to satisfy a desire to know, without any other motive. "Out of curiosity, I asked her what she did for a living."
  • "Satisfy one's curiosity" — to find the answer or information that your curiosity was demanding. "I had to read to the end of the article just to satisfy my curiosity."
  • "Pique someone's curiosity" / "spark curiosity" / "arouse curiosity" — to trigger curiosity in someone; to make them want to know more. "The mysterious locked box immediately piqued her curiosity."
  • "Overwhelmed by curiosity" — when the desire to know becomes so strong it is hard to resist. "Overwhelmed by curiosity, he opened the letter even though it was not addressed to him."
  • "Curiosity killed the cat" — a well-known English proverb that warns that being too curious — especially about things that are dangerous or none of your business — can get you into trouble. It is used to gently warn someone not to pry or take a risk simply to satisfy their curiosity.

Curiosity is considered one of the most important qualities a human being can have. Scientists, philosophers, artists, inventors, and great thinkers across history have pointed to curiosity as the starting point of all discovery and creativity. Without curiosity, there are no questions. Without questions, there is no learning. It is the single feeling that sits at the very beginning of almost all human knowledge.

At the same time, curiosity also has its social limits — there are things about which being curious is perfectly natural and encouraged, and things about which being curious can be considered intrusive or inappropriate.

What it isA desire to know, learn, or understand
How it feelsLike a pull, an itch, a gap that needs filling
What it doesDrives you to ask questions, explore, and discover
As a countable nounAn unusual or rare object/person/thing that attracts attention
At its bestIntellectual curiosity — open, eager, humble desire to understand
At its edgeNosiness, morbid curiosity — curiosity that oversteps or fixates on the dark

In short: curiosity is the feeling that says "I need to know more about this." It is what makes a child ask "why?" endlessly, what makes a scientist design an experiment, what makes a reader turn to the next page. It is one of the most human of all feelings — and one of the most valuable.
3818: "Curious" is a single word with two quite different meanings. Which meaning is being used depends entirely on what it is describing. Once you understand this split, the word becomes very easy to use.
Meaning 1 — Eager to Learn or Know

When "curious" describes a person (or a person's feeling), it means they have a desire to learn, discover, or understand something. A curious person is not satisfied with not knowing — they want to find out.

Think of it as a mental itch. Something catches your attention, and your mind wants to scratch it by getting more information.

Examples:

  • "She was curious about how the human brain works, so she read many books about it."

Here, she wanted to understand it. She wasn't content just not knowing.

  • "The child was curious about the strange box in the corner and kept looking at it."

The child felt a pull toward it — a desire to know what it was.

  • "He asked a lot of questions because he was naturally curious."

Here, "curious" describes a personality trait — he is the kind of person who always wants to learn and understand things in general, not just one specific thing.

Key point: Curiosity here is an active, internal feeling. It pushes a person toward exploration, questioning, and learning.

The construction "curious about": Very often, "curious" in this sense is followed by the word "about" + the thing the person wants to know.

  • Curious about science. Curious about a person. Curious about what happened.

You can also be curious to know something:

  • "I am curious to know what she said." (= I want to find out.)
Meaning 2 — Strange, Unusual, or Interesting in an Unexpected Way

When "curious" describes a thing, a situation, a fact, or an event, it means that thing is unusual, odd, or unexpectedly interesting. It stands out because it is not what you would normally expect.

This meaning does not describe a feeling. It describes a quality of the thing itself.

Examples:

  • "There was a curious smell coming from the kitchen."

The smell was strange and a bit unexpected — not an ordinary, easy-to-identify smell.

  • "It is a curious fact that some sharks have to keep swimming to stay alive."

The fact is surprising and interesting — not what most people would expect.

  • "He made a curious decision to leave right before the party started."

His decision was odd and hard to explain — it didn't follow what most people would do.

  • "A curious object sat on the shelf — no one knew what it was."

The object was unusual-looking and caught attention because it was different.

Key point: In this meaning, "curious" is a neutral word. It doesn't mean something is bad or good. It simply means it is noteworthy because it is unusual. It often carries a slight sense of "interesting" alongside "strange."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Look at what the word is describing:

Is it describing...Meaning
A person, or a person's feeling/stateEager to learn
A thing, fact, situation, or eventStrange or unusual
  • If "curious" describes a person or their feeling → they want to know something.
  • If "curious" describes a thing or a situation → it is strange or unusual.

For example:

  • "A curious scientist studied a curious creature."

The scientist is curious = she wants to learn. The creature is curious = it is strange and unusual.

Like most adjectives, "curious" can be made stronger or weaker:

  • A little curious — just slightly interested, mildly wanting to know.
  • Very curious / deeply curious / intensely curious — a strong, powerful desire to know.
  • Wildly curious — an almost uncontrollable urge to find out.

For the "strange" meaning:

  • A little curious — just slightly unusual.
  • Very curious / deeply curious / most curious — strikingly strange, very hard to explain.

• "Curious mind" — describes a person who naturally loves to learn and question things. "She has a curious mind — she never stops asking why."
  • "A curious case" — a situation or incident that is unusual and hard to explain. "It was a curious case — nobody knew how the money disappeared."
  • "Curiously enough" — used to introduce a fact that is surprising or unexpected. "Curiously enough, the two strangers had the same birthday." (Note: this is the adverb form, "curiously," but it helps you understand the flavour of the word.)

In real life, both meanings of "curious" carry a slightly positive or interesting tone:

  • A curious person is generally seen as a good thing — curiosity is associated with intelligence, openness, and a love of learning.
  • A curious thing is not necessarily scary or bad — it is more like something that makes you tilt your head and say, "Hm, that's interesting."

This is what separates "curious" from a word like "weird," which can feel more negative or judgmental. "Curious" is a more open, observational, and gentle word.

Since you will encounter the same word in other forms, here is a quick map:

  • Curiosity (noun) — the feeling of being curious (Meaning 1), or a strange and interesting object/thing (Meaning 2).
    "Her curiosity led her to explore the old library."
    "The shop was full of curiosities — old maps, ancient coins, and unusual ornaments."
  • Curiously (adverb) — in a curious way.
    "She looked at him curiously." (= with a wanting-to-know look.)
    "Curiously, no one mentioned the accident." (= strangely, interestingly.)

"Curious" means one of two things:

  1. A person who wants to learn or understand something — they feel a pull toward finding out. It is a quality of the mind and feeling.
  2. A thing that is strange, unusual, or unexpectedly interesting — it stands out from what is normal. It is a quality of the thing itself.

The context — specifically, whether the word is describing a person or a thing — tells you which meaning applies.
3819:
To curl up means to pull your body (or something) into a tight, rounded shape — like a ball or a C-shape — often for comfort, warmth, or rest.

Think of a sleeping cat. It doesn't stretch out flat. Instead, it tucks its head down, wraps its tail around itself, and folds into a small, round bundle. That is the perfect image of curling up.

The word curl means to bend or wind into a curve. The word up here doesn't mean "upward" — instead, it signals that the action is complete. You are fully coiled into that shape. Together, "curl up" means: to make yourself (or something) completely curved and compact.

This phrase is most commonly used to describe a person settling into a comfortable, relaxed position — usually on a sofa, a bed, or a chair — with their legs pulled up and their body hunched slightly inward.

Common patterns:

"Curl up with something" — This is the most frequent use. It means to get into a cozy, comfortable position while enjoying something:

  • She curled up with a good book and spent the whole afternoon reading.
  • He curled up with a cup of tea and watched the rain outside.

The "with" here suggests you are bringing that thing close to you as you settle in — almost like it's your companion.

"Curl up in bed / on the sofa / in a chair" — You settle into that place in a rounded, comfortable position:

  • After a long day, I just wanted to curl up in bed.
  • The child curled up on the sofa and fell asleep.

"Curl up in a ball" — This means pulling your knees to your chest and wrapping your arms around yourself, making your body as compact and round as a ball. This is often done when someone is very cold, very sad, or in pain:

  • It was freezing, so she curled up in a ball under the blanket.
  • He was so upset that he just curled up in a ball and cried.
When Animals and Things Curl Up

The phrase isn't only for people.

Animals curl up when they sleep or feel safe. Dogs, cats, hedgehogs — many animals instinctively curl up to conserve heat and protect their soft belly:

  • The dog curled up at his owner's feet.

Objects can also curl up, meaning they bend and fold inward — often because of heat, dryness, or age:

  • The old pages of the book had curled up at the edges.
  • The leaves curl up in summer heat.
  • The bacon started to curl up in the pan.

Notice that when used for objects, it loses the cozy feeling and just describes the physical bending.
The Feeling Behind the Phrase (for People)

When "curl up" is used about a person by choice, it almost always carries a warm, cozy, safe feeling. It suggests peace, rest, and comfort — wanting to be small and snug in a pleasant way.

However, when someone curls up because of pain, cold, grief, or fear, the feeling shifts. It suggests vulnerability — the body protecting itself by making itself small:

  • She curled up in pain after the fall.
  • He curled up under his blanket and refused to talk to anyone.

So context matters. The body position is the same, but the emotion behind it can be either contentment or distress.
The Special Expression: "Curl Up and Die"

This is a very common idiom. It does not mean someone actually wants to die. It means someone feels so embarrassed, ashamed, or mortified that they wish they could disappear completely from the world.

  • When I called the teacher "Mum" by accident, I wanted to curl up and die.
  • He said the wrong thing at the wrong moment and just wanted to curl up and die.

You can also say "it makes me want to curl up and die" about something deeply cringe-worthy.

"Curl up" is a phrasal verb — a verb + particle combination that works as a unit.

It is mostly intransitive, meaning it doesn't need an object:

  • ✅ She curled up. (no object needed)

But you can also use it transitively with an object — to describe curling something else:

  • ✅ She curled her fingers up into a fist.
  • ✅ The heat curled the paper up.

The past tense is simply curled up:

  • He curled up on the couch last night.

The present continuous (curling up) is also very common:

  • Stop curling up your toes like that.
  • She's curling up with a movie tonight.

SituationMeaning
  • Person + sofa/bed + book/movie → relaxing comfortably in a cozy, rounded position
  • Person + ball → body folded tightly, often due to cold, pain, or sadness
  • Animal → sleeping in a compact, rounded shape
  • Object (leaves, paper) → bending or folding inward, usually from heat or dryness
  • "Curl up and die" → feeling so embarrassed you wish you could disappear

• On cold winter nights, there's nothing better than curling up by the fire.
  • The kitten curled up in her lap and purred.
  • I was so embarrassed by what I said — I could have curled up and died.
  • The edges of the photograph had curled up from the humidity.
  • She curled up under the blanket, too tired to even take off her shoes.

The heart of the phrase is always the same image: something bending inward into a curved, compact shape. Whether it's a person finding comfort, an animal sleeping, or a leaf drying out — that rounded, self-contained shape is what "curl up" always describes.
